content: After birth, it is common in standard hospital care for mothers and their newborns to be separated. Typically, newborns are either wrapped or dressed and held in their mother’s arms, placed in open cribs, or kept under radiant warmers. Skin-to-skin contact (SSC), however, ideally begins immediately after birth and continues uninterrupted until the first breastfeeding session is completed. SSC involves placing the dried, naked infant in a prone position directly on the mother’s bare chest, often covered with a warm blanket. From a mammalian neuroscience perspective, this intimate contact triggers neuro-behaviors that fulfill essential biological needs. The period immediately following birth may represent a critical sensitive period for programming the infant's future physiological and behavioral development. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of immediate or early SSC compared to standard care on breastfeeding initiation and maintenance, as well as on infant physiological outcomes. To gather data, researchers searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of December 17, 2015), contacted trial authors, consulted a bibliography on kangaroo mother care (KMC) maintained by Dr. Susan Ludington, and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The analysis included randomized controlled trials comparing immediate or early SSC with standard hospital care. Two reviewers independently assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified accuracy. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 46 trials involving 3,850 women and their infants, with 38 trials (3,472 participants) contributing data to the analysis. These trials were conducted in 21 countries, though most had small sample sizes (only 12 trials included more than 100 participants). Eight trials involved women who underwent cesarean deliveries. All infants included in the trials were healthy, with the majority being full-term. Six trials included late preterm infants (gestational age >35 weeks). None of the trials met all criteria for high methodological and reporting quality. Blinding was not achieved in any trial, and the analyses were imprecise due to small sample sizes. Additionally, there was significant statistical heterogeneity between SSC and standard care groups. Findings for Mothers: Women who practiced SSC were more likely to be breastfeeding at one to four months postpartum compared to those receiving standard care. However, this finding was somewhat uncertain due to potential biases in the included trials (average risk ratio [RR] 1.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07 to 1.43; participants = 887; studies = 14; I² = 41%; GRADE: moderate quality). SSC mothers breastfed for a longer duration, though the data were limited (mean difference [MD] 64 days, 95% CI 37.96 to 89.50; participants = 264; studies = 6; GRADE: low quality). This result was derived from a sensitivity analysis that excluded one trial contributing to heterogeneity in the primary analysis. SSC mothers were more likely to exclusively breastfeed from hospital discharge to one month postpartum and from six weeks to six months postpartum. However, both analyses showed substantial heterogeneity (from discharge: average RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.49; participants = 711; studies = 6; I² = 44%; GRADE: moderate quality; from six weeks: average RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.90; participants = 640; studies = 7; I² = 62%; GRADE: moderate quality). Women in the SSC group had higher mean scores for breastfeeding effectiveness, as measured by the Infant Breastfeeding Assessment Tool (IBFAT), with moderate heterogeneity (MD 2.28, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.15; participants = 384; studies = 4; I² = 41%). SSC infants were more likely to breastfeed successfully during their first feeding session, though there was high heterogeneity in the data (average RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.67; participants = 575; studies = 5; I² = 85%). Findings for Infants: Infants in the SSC group had higher SCRIP (stability of the cardio-respiratory system) scores, indicating better stabilization of three physiological parameters. However, the clinical significance of this finding was unclear due to the small number of infants and the use of averaged data from multiple time points (standardized mean difference [SMD] 1.24, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.72; participants = 81; studies = 2; GRADE: low quality). SSC infants had higher blood glucose levels compared to those in standard care (MD 10.49 mg/dL, 95% CI 8.39 to 12.59; participants = 144; studies = 3; GRADE: low quality). There was no significant difference in body temperature between SSC infants and those receiving standard care (MD 0.30°C, 95% CI 0.13°C to 0.47°C; participants = 558; studies = 6; I² = 88%; GRADE: low quality). Findings for Women and Infants After Cesarean Birth: Women practicing SSC after cesarean delivery were more likely to breastfeed at one to four months postpartum and to breastfeed successfully, as measured by IBFAT scores. However, these analyses were based on only two trials with small sample sizes. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether SSC improved breastfeeding outcomes at other time points following cesarean delivery. Single trials contributed data on infant respiratory rate, maternal pain, and maternal anxiety, but these trials lacked sufficient power to detect differences between groups. Subgroup Analyses: No significant differences were found in outcomes when comparing the timing of SSC initiation (immediate initiation within 10 minutes of birth versus early initiation after 10 minutes) or the duration of SSC (60 minutes or less versus more than 60 minutes). Conclusions: The evidence supports the use of SSC to promote breastfeeding. However, larger studies are needed to confirm the physiological benefits of SSC for infants during the transition to extra-uterine life and to determine the optimal timing and duration of SSC. The methodological quality of the included trials was problematic, with small sample sizes, inconsistent outcome measures, and limited data, which reduce confidence in the reported benefits of SSC for infants. Additionally, the review only included healthy infants, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other populations and makes interpretation of physiological outcomes more challenging.
